title: "Experiences and Change"
subtitle: "When do people's life experiences change their attitudes and values?"

![Figure S4 from Brandt et al.](../img/proj-lifeexperiences.png){.project-figure fig-alt="Figure S4 from Brandt et al."}



Adult political attitudes are highly stable (Brandt & Morgan, 2022; Turner-Zwinkels & Brandt, 2025), but they do change. What kinds of experiences make people change their attitudes? One idea in the literature is that experiences that cause people to feel threatened and uncertain may cause attitude and value change. Typical approaches predict that when people experience threat they turn to conservative political attitudes. This is because the resistance to change and deference to authority found in many conservative attitudes may help people cope with the uncertainty experienced with a threat.

Our work has found that this typical approach makes inaccurate predictions because the link between life experiences and attitude and value change is inconsistent (for a review see Brandt & Bakker, 2022). For example, in a study of over 50 countries, we find that the link between perceived threats and political attitudes varies by the specific threat (e.g., of violence, economic downturns, the police), the specific political attitudes (e.g., economic attitudes, cultural attitudes), and the country (Brandt et al., 2021). The variability extends to individuals. Using panel data, we estimated how the onset of the pandemic affected people’s attitudes and values (Brandt et al., 2025). We found only a few overall changes, but we also found substantial unexplained variability around these average effects. That is, threatening life experiences do not shape attitudes and values in the same way for all people. At the same time, we do not have good explanations for this variability. In a recent paper, we lab explored how personality traits might moderate the effects of societal changes (e.g., unemployment, increased immigration) on political attitudes (Cassario & Brandt, 2025), but personality traits were not important for understanding this variation.

Future projects aim to comprehensively map how life experiences are related to changes and stability in political attitudes. There is a lot of existing data on these questions that is currently untapped. Therefore, our lab is in the process of identifying as many existing panel studies as possible from as many countries as possible that measure people’s political attitudes and their life experiences. We will then integrate these panels to comprehensively test how life experiences (e.g.. loss of income, a new child) shape attitudes and values. We anticipate that this integrated panel project will help us tackle our questions about life experiences and attitude change, but will also be valuable for any scholars interested in how attitude change over the life course.
